html:
One of the oldest churches in Rome, in the Trastevere district across the Tiber, and by its own inscription the first in the city dedicated to the Virgin Mary, a claim Santa Maria Maggiore also makes. By tradition Pope Callixtus I founded a house church here about 220, on the site of a refuge for retired soldiers, after the emperor Severus Alexander settled a quarrel between the Christians and the tavern keepers in the Christians' favour. Pope Julius I rebuilt it on a larger scale in 340, and after restorations in the 5th and 8th centuries it was raised again on its old foundations in 1140 to 1143 under Pope Innocent II, who is buried here.

The nave keeps the old basilica plan. Its 22 granite columns were taken from the ruins of the Baths of Caracalla; their capitals bore faces of the Egyptian gods Isis, Serapis and Harpocrates until a restoration under Pius IX in 1870 hammered them off. The apse mosaic of the Coronation of the Virgin, made in 1130 to 1143, shows Innocent II holding a model of the church, and below it run mosaics of the Life of the Virgin by Pietro Cavallini, from 1291. A chapel holds the Madonna della Clemenza, an icon painted in hot wax between the 6th and 9th centuries, probably Byzantine, one of the oldest surviving images of Mary. Domenichino designed the gilded ceiling and painted its Assumption in 1617.

Outside, the 12th-century Romanesque bell tower stands over the square, and high on the front a 13th-century mosaic shows Mary nursing the Child between ten women holding lamps. Carlo Fontana rebuilt the porch in 1702 and restored the octagonal fountain in the square, which already appears on a map of 1472. The church has been a cardinal's title church since at least the 3rd century.
